summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: A.A. ex rel. Lewis v. Shutts
key_cases.holding: The court held that KRS 620.050(1) immunity is available only to a person who acts by making a report, so a physician who did not report suspected abuse of a foster child later murdered by his foster uncle was not immune, and it reversed summary judgment because a jury could find she breached her KRS 620.030 duty to report.
key_cases.relevance: This is Kentucky's principal published civil-liability decision arising from the death of a child in a Cabinet foster placement.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the Immunity Statute only applies to those who act by making a report

key_cases.holding: In a mother's negligence and wrongful-death action against DCBS social workers after her child's death, the court reversed summary judgment on qualified official immunity because the circuit court made no findings identifying the source or nature of the workers' duties, and remanded for the specific findings Meinhart requires on the ministerial/discretionary question.
key_cases.relevance: This is the most recent published Kentucky decision on whether DCBS workers can be held personally liable for a child's death on their caseload.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court's order granting summary judgment did not contain any findings identifying the nature or source of the defendants' duties and why it believed these duties were discretionary

key_cases.case_name: Cabinet for Health & Family Services v. Todd County Standard, Inc.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed enforcement of an unappealed Attorney General open-records decision requiring the Cabinet to produce records about a child who died under circumstances suggesting abuse, held that statutory authority for a record's creation raises a rebuttable presumption that it exists, and upheld the finding that the Cabinet's denial was willful.
key_cases.relevance: The case concerns the Cabinet's mandatory internal review under KRS 620.050(1)(b) of a child fatality where it had prior involvement with the family.
key_cases.quote: The Cabinet cannot benefit from intentionally frustrating the Attorney General's review of an open records request
